claims.text: GeoDeploy pairs TypeSafe Jev's confidence-scored decisions with the Pulumi Automation API to place and scale Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
GeoDeploy (pulumi/devx-geodeploy) is released as open source.
GeoDeploy prices and compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes.
GeoDeploy asks Jev to pick the best region per geo from a closed list of already-priced candidates, so Jev cannot select a hallucinated region.
GeoDeploy gates every Jev decision on a confidence threshold, with a hard reject for data-residency failures.
GeoDeploy provisions consistent clusters using one Pulumi stack per region.
GeoDeploy's self-driving mode scales deployments on its own, with a human in the loop for approval when Jev's confidence is low.
TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, which is their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (published 2026-09-25).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev provides a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are the perfect complement to agentic work.
Combining Jev's reasoning with Pulumi makes the gap between designing ideal infrastructure and deploying it to production practically vanish.
Agents can now handle infrastructure provisioning and day-to-day scaling and reliability decisions.

A GeoDeploy deployment request has four parts: target geos (traffic share per place and data-residency rule: EU-only, US-only, or in-country), a container image with target platforms (amd64, arm64, or both), a workload shape (replicas, CPU and memory per pod, egress, storage), and constraints (allowed providers, max number of providers, budget).
GeoDeploy picks the best region for each geo and provisions consistent environments across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing, does all the math, and never makes judgment calls.
In GeoDeploy, Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use, and never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names.
In GeoDeploy, Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS and decides nothing.
GeoDeploy maps each business region (geo) to a canonical location and residency class.
GeoDeploy lists every region with managed Kubernetes as a candidate and uses great-circle distance as its coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches live prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy uses plain deterministic TypeScript to bin-pack pods onto nodes, filter out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and compute a monthly cost per candidate.
In GeoDeploy, Jev picks the winning region and modules for each geo.
GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy will not run provisioning unless the user's cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
The link target /automation/ exists as a Pulumi Automation API page on the Pulumi website.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md containing the full decision record.
GeoDeploy includes a web UI that shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev doesn't return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives.
Jev's `choice()` primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's `score()` primitive rates something against a rubric you describe; GeoDeploy's rubrics use 10 levels.
Jev's `noul()` primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Because Jev only selects from closed sets and never writes code or does arithmetic, a hallucinated region such as `us-west-9` or a made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates along with the constraints and the image's architecture.

In a single call per geo, GeoDeploy asks Jev for a region selection (choice), five quality scores (score: coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (noul: data residency satisfied, enough capacity), and a fallback backup region (choice).
The GeoDeploy repository contains a file at packages/decide/src/questions.ts that builds the Stage A questions.
The `choice`, `noul`, and `score` functions are exported by the `@typesafe-ai/sdk` package.
TypeSafe advises rubrics to "describe situations, not degrees."

GeoDeploy's score rubric levels are concrete scenarios running from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" up to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."
The options passed to `choice()` are the priced candidates keyed by ID, so Jev can't answer with a region that isn't on the list.

The TypeSafe SDK exposes a `TypeSafeClient` class whose `systemOne({ state, questions })` method returns a result with an `answers` object exposing `selection.choice`, `selection.confidence`, `residencyOk.noul`, and `coverage.score`.
GeoDeploy's five scores feed a ranking system using weight profiles: latency-optimized (the default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because GeoDeploy's ranking weights live in code, the ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.
In GeoDeploy's composite ranking score, sprawl risk is subtracted rather than added.
Every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.

In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), and Jev decides only ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier via a second, smaller set of questions.
GeoDeploy checks every Jev answer against a confidence threshold matched to the risk of the decision.
GeoDeploy's data-residency confidence threshold is 0.95, and failing it causes a hard reject.
GeoDeploy's confidence threshold for choosing a region for a new cluster is 0.90; if it isn't met, the top three candidates are flagged for a human to choose.
GeoDeploy's confidence threshold for choosing a region when a stack already exists is 0.75; if it isn't met, the existing region is kept.
GeoDeploy's confidence threshold for Jev's ingress or autoscaling module choice is 0.85; if it isn't met, the registry default is used.
GeoDeploy's confidence threshold for Jev's node-pool sizing tier is 0.60; if it isn't met, the bin-packing result is used.
GeoDeploy has a global confidence floor of 0.50 for region pick, residency, or capacity answers; if it isn't met, the AI path is dropped for that geo.
The GeoDeploy repository contains packages/decide/src/engine.ts, which enforces the residency gate and validates that the selection is one of the candidates.
GeoDeploy's confidence gate enforcement is plain deterministic code that hard-rejects below the residency threshold and throws AiPathAborted when Jev selects an unknown candidate ID.
Each `AiPathAborted` error in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or returns an error, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing the residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.
When self-driving mode is enabled with `geodeploy monitor`, the agent periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization.

In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, the agent asks Jev one joint question across all regions with the answers `no-change`, `scale-up:<geo>`, `scale-down:<geo>`, or `shift:<from>-><to>`, plus a separate check on disruption risk.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, code, not Jev, computes the actual node-count changes.

In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, resizes are applied automatically above 0.85 confidence, suggested for human approval between 0.70 and 0.85, and below 0.70 GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.

CPU utilization alone is a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency, error rates, or application-specific metrics once a traffic baseline is established.
To get started with GeoDeploy you need access to Jev and a cloud provider.
The GitHub repository pulumi/devx-geodeploy exists and contains GeoDeploy.
The Pulumi Automation API docs exist at /docs/iac/automation-api/.
TypeSafe Jev documentation exists at https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction.
Pulumi's X account handle is @PulumiCorp at https://x.com/PulumiCorp.
A free Pulumi account can be signed up for at https://app.pulumi.com/signup.
